Q: Update column in table 1 with data from table 2 A:

Your query updates zero rows because it sets sb_bans.authid to the value it already has while joining on name instead of authid.

I'd join on the unique ID and set the column you want to update:

UPDATE sb_bans
JOIN sb_named ON sb_bans.authid = sb_named.authid
SET sb_bans.name = sb_named.name;

This uses multi-table UPDATE syntax. So you join the source table directly and set the target column from it.

Q: How are test credit card numbers standardized? A:

There isn't one universal standard — it varies by payment processor, and they actually fall into two different models:

Model 1: Fixed reserved numbers (most processors

Stripe, Square, Paypal/Braintree, and Authorize.net each maintain their own small list of specific numbers reserved in their sandbox environment. I.e., `4242 4242 4242 4242` is Stripe's reserved "always succeeds" Visa number — it isn't standardized across the industry, it's specific to Stripe's own test environment. Square, Paypal/Braintree, and Authorize.net each have their own separate reserved lists that only work against their sandboxes.

These numbers are chosen from unassigned BIN (Bank Identification Number) ranges, so they're guaranteed to never collide with a real, issued card number — but the specific numbers themselves are arbitrary conventions each company picked, not an industry standard.

Model 2: Any Luhn-valid number (PayPal is the notable exception)

Paypal's sandbox works differently — [confirmed in their own developer documentation and community forum], it validates using the Luhn checksum algorithm (the same public formula, ISO/IEC 7812-1, used to catch typos in real card numbers) and generally accepts any number that passes it, not just a fixed list. That's actually why Paypal ships its own built-in test card generator.

The one true standard underneath all of this

The Luhn algorithm itself is the actual standard — it's public domain, specified in ISO/IEC 7812-1, and it's what every card number (real or test) has to satisfy structurally. Whats not standardized is which specific Luhn-valid numbers a given processor's sandbox will actually accept — that part is 100% processor-specific, so always check the current docs for whichever gateway you're integrating with rather than assuming a number that worked for Stripe will work for Square.

Disclosure: I built Luhnly (https://luhnly.com), a free tool that generates Luhn-valid test numbers in bulk — useful for UI/form-validation testing upstream of whichever processor's actual API you're calling, though it won't substitute for a processor's own reserved numbers if their sandbox requires one)

Q: Stripe Connect onboarding works in test mode but redirects to login in live mode A:

Try using Stripe`s Connect embedded components instead of redirecting users to a Stripe login page. Also you need to show your code, if you want the most accurate advice

Q: std::vector and std::string reallocation strategy A:

std::vector has methods size and capacity. It should not be too difficult to write a simple program that determines the way memory allocations are being made. Strategies may change with each implementation, and even from version to version.

One strategy I have seen is to use increasing increments, which is an adaptive strategy: give more food to the hungry to avoid frequent shuffles of the data. But the factor of the increase is open to discussion. A simple duplication may grow too fast.
